executive_summary: CAD/JPY closed at 110.77 on 2026-10-02 in the gated price store. The pair is quoted in yen per Canadian dollar, so a falling pair means a stronger yen. It is down 1.94% over one month, 2.98% over three months and 3.74% over six months, but still 2.87% higher than a year ago, which puts it at the 37th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 107.04–117.24. The main bilateral story is that the +100bp policy gap is the pair's only fundamental support, and it is set to narrow from both ends. The Bank of Japan has hiked 50bp in 2026 and has three decisions before end-January. The Bank of Canada has held at 2.25% for seven meetings, with an operational core inflation rate of 1.95% and a Canadian two-year yield that carries 112bp of hike premium its own reaction function does not support. Neither standalone dossier nets the commodity effect. Canada exports energy and Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil, so terms of trade is the one factor arguing for a higher pair. That support is capped, though: Canada realises only about USD 76.70 a barrel against the roughly USD 100 Brent price Japan pays. The settled verdict is Bearish on both horizons. Tactically it is conviction 2 at a net score of -0.102, just two thousandths past the Bearish threshold. Strategically it is conviction 3 at -0.2887. Both legs resolve in one double event: the Bank of Canada's Monetary Policy Report on 2026-10-28 and the Bank of Japan's Outlook Report on 2026-10-30. The chart agrees with that direction, but it is not the basis for it: spot sits 244–363 pips below a fully inverted 50/100/200-day average stack after five lower highs since April. The main caveat is location. Spot is only 39 pips above a two-touch shelf and 131 pips above the eight-touch 108.92–110.00 band, the densest support on the chart. So the tactical edge lies in selling rallies into the three-touch 111.41–112.16 zone rather than chasing spot. A short also pays about 10 pips a month in futures roll, speculators are already crowded short the pair (short CAD and long JPY at the same time), and published forecast paths sit flat to higher at 110–114.

market_context.valuation_assessment: No pair-level PPP series exists, so both dossiers proxy valuation from BIS real effective exchange rates: CAD at 96.29 and JPY at 66.02 for August 2026. At 110.77 the pair prices a persistent Japanese funding disadvantage and a Canadian trade discount at the same time. It does not price the hedged-yield crossover that is pulling Japanese money home. tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +100bp in CAD's favour: the Bank of Canada Overnight Rate Target is 2.25%, held for a seventh consecutive meeting on 2026-09-02, against a Bank of Japan call rate of 1.25% after the 7-2 hike of 2026-09-18. That gap has narrowed 25bp in a fortnight and the direction of travel is one-way: the BoC is the only one of the two with no hike delivered in 2026, while the BoJ has moved 50bp this year. At the ten-year point the payload's monthly vintages show CAD 3.675% against JPY 2.94%, a +73.5bp spread, and on live prints the Government of Canada 10-year at 3.96% against a JGB 10-year of 3.06% is +90bp — a gap that has compressed sharply as the JGB 10-year rose 141bp over twelve months. The transmission is carry and expected carry: a long CAD/JPY position earns roughly 110 pips a year of policy carry at 110.77 spot, and that is the entire fundamental case for holding the pair higher. Both legs decide inside the tactical window — the BoC on 2026-10-28 with a Monetary Policy Report and the BoJ on 2026-10-30 with an Outlook Report, two days apart, with the Canadian decision setting the tone first. The asymmetry in what each bank has to deliver against its own curve is what makes this Bearish rather than Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the question is not the level of the +100bp differential but its first derivative, and both legs point the same way. The BoJ holds three scheduled decisions inside the window — 2026-10-30 and 2027-01-22 with Outlook Reports and 2026-12-18 without — each a forecast round at which the terminal rate can be marked up; its own guidance is to continue raising rates. The BoC holds two, on 2026-10-28 with a Monetary Policy Report and on 2026-12-09, with policy at the very bottom of its 2.25-3.25% neutral band but an operational core of 1.95%, employment down 41,700 in August and a tariff regime that escalated to outright import bans on 2026-09-29. Two BoJ hikes against a BoC hold compresses the bilateral differential from 100bp to 50bp; one of each leaves it at 100bp. The distribution of outcomes is skewed because the Canadian curve carries 112bp of hike premium above the policy rate in a two-year at 3.37% that the Bank's own reaction function does not support, while Japanese pricing of roughly 39% for December leaves room to reprice upward. Term structure compounds it: the JGB 10-year has risen 141bp in a year and now trades above the Bund, so Japan has stopped being the funding sovereign of last resort, which erodes the structural bid for yen-funded long-CAD positions independently of the policy rate.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On headline the inflation differential is +110bp in Canada's favour, 3.0% against Japan's 1.9%, but on each central bank's own operational measure the gap nearly vanishes: the BoC trim-median average is 1.95% and the BoJ core ex fresh food is 1.7%, a 25bp spread between two economies whose underlying inflation is at or below target. Growth favours Canada marginally, 1.13% year-on-year against 0.73%, and Canada's Q2 annualised 3.3% beats Japan's 1.4%, but both series are decelerating and the composition is poor on both sides — Canadian employment fell 41,700 in August with wage growth halved to 2.0%, while Japanese private consumption contributed exactly zero to Q2 GDP and household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year. The surprise flow is genuinely two-sided: Canada's September tally ran eight negative against six positive with the negatives in activity and the positives in prices, while Japan missed on the Tankan at +24 and on industrial production at -1.7% but beat on PPI at 7.6% and services prices at 3.7%. Over four weeks the asymmetric sensitivity sits on the Canadian side, because the 2026-10-09 labour report and the 2026-10-19 CPI are both higher-variance for the pair than anything Japan publishes in the window. With the two data flows mirroring each other in shape, this is a genuine Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two inflation processes move in opposite directions and the pair is on the wrong side of both. Canada's headline decays mechanically: gasoline at +22.8% year-on-year cannot persist with WTI at USD 91.51 against a Reuters 2026 consensus of USD 83.90, so headline converges toward the 2.4% ex-gasoline rate and then the 1.95% trim-median average, removing the public rationale for BoC tightening. Japan's suppressed core does the reverse: electricity is held down 2.4% by government subsidy while producer prices run at 7.6%, a 5.9-point pipeline sitting on the government's balance sheet with an expiry date, and Tankan three-year-ahead corporate inflation expectations are at 2.6% with Shunto settled at 5.01% for a fourth consecutive year. The growth differential also deteriorates against Canada: Macklem has put Q4 growth 'below 1%' if tariffs persist, and they have escalated to import bans, while Japan's narrow but real AI-semiconductor export cycle lifted electronic components 52.3%. The transmission to CAD/JPY is through relative policy response — converging Canadian inflation against firming Japanese inflation pulls the rate differential toward compression on both legs at once, which is the pair's dominant driver.

CAD's equity beta of -0.2 to -0.3 against the S&P 500 is the weakest in the commodity bloc, so the Canadian leg contributes little, while the yen leg is the dominant risk transmission and has not needed it: the yen beat every G10 currency over the month in a tape where equities held, which says September's move was policy and positioning rather than fear. Gold down 6.0% over the month and an intact Iran ceasefire both point to a draining rather than a rebuilding crisis premium. The oil complication is specific to this pair and cuts both ways — a supply-driven crude rally is CAD-positive and JPY-negative but is not a risk-on signal, so the usual correlation reading fails. Net: no tactical direction.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months speculative positioning normalises on both legs and institutional flow takes over, and that flow is asymmetric against the pair. factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised from 0.06 to 0.10 tactically and from 0.16 to 0.18 strategically. This is a net energy exporter against an economy importing roughly 99% of its oil and 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East, in a year when Brent is up 53.6%. The terms-of-trade axis carries more of this pair's fundamental content than any other bilateral pair in the CAD or JPY complex, and it is the only factor arguing for a higher pair on both horizons.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The terms-of-trade differential is the clearest structural argument for a higher CAD/JPY and it is working now. Canada's Q2 current account swung to a C$8.8bn surplus on record energy exports of C$60.6bn, its first since 2022-Q2, while Japan posted a 1,105.6bn yen goods deficit in August, a fourth consecutive monthly deficit and the largest since January, with crude oil imports up 58.7% and total mineral fuels up 38.4%. Brent near USD 100 is a transfer from Japan to Canada at the aggregate level. Two qualifications are material and they cap rather than reverse the signal. First, Canada realises WTI less a USD 14.80 WCS discount against a Brent-WTI spread of USD 11.05, so its barrel prints near USD 76.70 against a USD 100.17 headline — it captures perhaps three quarters of the move Japan pays in full. Second, Japan's headline current account remains in surplus at 5.03% of GDP, but that surplus is primary income reinvested offshore while the FX-generative goods line is in deficit, which is the part that settles in spot. Bilateral trade itself is immaterial as a flow: CAD reports exports of 10.9bn dollars to Japan against imports of 16.2bn, a 5.2bn deficit, on IMF DOTS 2024 data, against Japan-reported figures of 11.2bn and 13.0bn — small in both directions and asymmetrically recorded.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At an 0.18 weight this is the largest single offset to the bearish case and the assessment is finely balanced but net positive for the pair. Japan's energy import bill is a structural transfer that does not require oil to rise further — at a flat USD 98-100 Brent the goods deficit persists every month, and HSBC describes Hormuz as structurally impaired with DBS assuming no resolution within three to six months. Canada's position is the mirror image at a lower amplitude: a real surplus, but one whose capture is capped by pipeline takeaway, with the WCS discount a standing tax and no new approval inside the horizon, and one that the Reuters September poll expects to erode as WTI converges on USD 83.90. The netting therefore gives CAD a clear but bounded advantage. Against that sit two real drags on the Canadian side that have no Japanese counterpart — Section 338 import bans live since 2026-09-29 and a USMCA now on annual review cycles through 2036 — and one Japanese offset, the AI semiconductor cycle that lifted electronic component exports 52.3%. Comparatively, Canada's +1.03% of GDP is mid-table while Japan's +5.03% is fifth-highest in the set, so on the headline measure the pair is pointed the wrong way; it is the composition, not the level, that makes this Bullish.

The confidence does not rise with the weight because the Canadian side of the differential is expected to erode on the consensus oil path.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: CAD: net energy exporter. Crude oil and bitumen at a record C$44.8bn of quarterly exports, total energy exports C$60.6bn. Realisation is WTI at Hardisty less a USD 14.80 WCS discount, not Brent. Henry Hub at USD 2.90 provides no secondary support. Direction rule: oil up is ++CAD, applied here at reduced strength because of the discount structure.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY: among the most energy-import-dependent economies in the set, importing roughly 99% of its oil and 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East, and a major LNG importer exposed to JKM. Direction rules: oil up is --JPY and LNG up is --JPY, both applied at full strength because Japan pays the waterborne price with no domestic offset.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Apply the framework rules in sequence. Oil up gives ++CAD and --JPY, which for a pair quoted as yen per Canadian dollar is unambiguously bullish — both legs push the same way. The amplitude is then adjusted for realisation: Canada captures WTI at USD 91.51 less USD 14.80 of WCS discount, roughly USD 76.70, against a Brent headline of USD 100.17 that Japan effectively pays, so the Canadian benefit is roughly three quarters of the Japanese cost per barrel of move. LNG is a pure one-sided negative for the yen with no Canadian export offset inside the horizon, which adds to the pair. Netting across both commodities: oil up is strongly bullish CAD/JPY, oil down is strongly bearish, and the asymmetry is modestly in the pair's favour on the way up because Japan has no hedge against the import bill while Canada at least retains the revenue above its discount.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent from roughly 100 to 110. Japanese monthly goods deficit widens materially on a 58.7%-growth crude import line while Canadian energy export values rise less than proportionately because the WCS discount is a fixed dollar wedge. Net: bullish CAD/JPY, and the single most reliable positive scenario for the pair. It would also restore the Bank of Canada's own stated precondition for expecting inflation to edge up, adding a rate-channel positive on top.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent from roughly 100 to 90, toward the Reuters USD 89.05 2026 consensus. Japan's goods deficit narrows sharply and the terms-of-trade transfer reverses, while Canada's current account shrinks toward C$2-5bn and the gasoline base effect that supports a 3.0% headline CPI collapses faster. Net: bearish CAD/JPY on both the flow and the rate channel, and because the consensus oil path is below spot this is the modal rather than the tail case.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil, but specifically the WTI-versus-Brent relationship rather than the headline. Canada is paid WTI less WCS and Japan pays waterborne Brent and JKM, so the pair's true commodity driver is the Brent-WTI spread as much as the level — at USD 11.05, nearly triple a year ago, the spread is transferring a third of the pair's notional commodity support away from the Canadian dollar.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Guidance divergence is the cleanest bilateral signal in the dossier and it points down for the pair. The Bank of Canada's hawkish turn is conditional and the condition has failed: Governor Macklem told a Halifax audience on 2026-09-21 that if oil prices stay near USD 100 a barrel the Bank would expect inflation to edge up, and WTI closed at USD 91.51 on 2026-09-30 with a Reuters 2026 consensus of USD 83.90. Governing Council held unanimously on 2026-09-02 and found little evidence of gasoline pass-through to other prices. The Bank of Japan's guidance is unconditional in the other direction — it has said it will continue raising rates as underlying inflation approaches 2%, and the Summary of Opinions released 2026-09-30 shows a majority favouring further hikes with one member arguing to accelerate. The two vehicles land two days apart: a Monetary Policy Report on 2026-10-28 at which Canada must publish an oil assumption against the Governor's own threshold and debut a new inflation model, then an Outlook Report on 2026-10-30 at which Japan can mark up its CPI path. Sequence matters — the Canadian walk-back sets the tone before the Japanese upgrade arrives, so the two events compound rather than offset for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the institutional cadences diverge as sharply as the messages. The BoJ has three forecast opportunities inside the window — Outlook Reports on 2026-10-30 and 2027-01-22 and a decision on 2026-12-18 — and has now delivered two hikes in 2026 against an expansionary Takaichi administration widely assumed to prefer accommodation, which is the strongest available evidence on its independence. The Bank of Canada has two decisions, one with a Monetary Policy Report, and must reconcile a credible but conditional hiking bias with a core measure below target, excess supply, unemployment near 6.4% and wage growth halved to 2.0%. Credibility is not symmetric in quality: Canada's communication architecture is the more legible, with quarterly reports, a two-week Summary of Deliberations and a published neutral-rate estimate, while the BoJ remains the most opaque central bank in the G10 — but legibility works against the Canadian dollar here, because the market can see precisely how far the curve has run beyond the reaction function. A separate Japanese guidance channel has no Canadian counterpart: the Ministry of Finance and the US Treasury have jointly confirmed the late-July coordinated intervention and signalled readiness to repeat it, which is forward guidance on the exchange rate itself.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk is asymmetric against the pair because the Canadian leg carries a live shock and the Japanese leg carries an official floor. US Section 338 measures escalated from a 50% ad valorem duty to outright import bans effective 2026-09-29, two days before the valuation date, against roughly C$20bn of Canadian retaliation imposed 2026-09-08, with USMCA providing no relief and the duties stacking on existing measures. That damage will show in the 2026-10-06 trade print and the 2026-10-09 labour report, neither of which is priced. On the Japanese side the late-July 2026 coordinated US-Japan intervention — the first joint operation since 2011, roughly 8.45 trillion yen from Japan with a US Treasury contribution — demonstrated a two-government commitment that Finance Minister Katayama has said will be repeated if needed. That put was aimed at USD/JPY but transmits to every yen cross, so the left tail for the yen is truncated and the right tail for CAD/JPY is capped in a way that has no Canadian equivalent. Clustering is dense and one-sided: Canada publishes trade, labour and CPI inside the window while Japan's only comparable release is the 2026-10-07 current account.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the Canadian political risk is architectural rather than episodic. The United States declined the 16-year USMCA extension at the 2026-07-01 joint review, so the agreement now runs on annual review cycles through a 2036 expiry — converting a settled treaty into a perpetually renegotiated one for an economy sending 66.3% of its goods exports to one counterparty. That is the most plausible single explanation for a Canadian REER that fell 1.67 points over twelve months while Australia's rose 9.97 and Norway's 7.84, and it is a standing risk premium rather than a shock. The Japanese side carries the opposite structure: a coordinated intervention put that truncates the yen's weak tail without truncating its strong one, offset by an expansionary Takaichi administration whose FY2027 budget lands in December with Fitch publicly committed to reviewing it. The one dated de-escalation catalyst is USTR's end-2026 target for interim USMCA deals, which is the principal upside risk to this stance and the reason confidence sits at 55 rather than higher. Geopolitically, a Hormuz re-escalation is the one tail that would push the pair up, because it bids the yen on haven flow but taxes Japan's terms of trade harder than it taxes Canada's.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The sovereign differential is wide and entirely static over four weeks. Canada carries Aaa from Moody's, AAA from S&P and DBRS and AA+ from Fitch, all stable, against Japan's A1, A+ and A, also all stable — a three-to-four-notch gap that has been in place for years and has no dated catalyst inside the window on either side. Debt levels are not comparable: Canadian federal debt near 42% of GDP and general government near 92% against a Japanese stock near 260%, though Japan's is roughly 90% domestically held with about half absorbed by its own central bank. Both curves are orderly. Canada's 2s10s at +59bp with a long bond at 4.25% shows no risk premium, and Japanese auctions are clearing — the late-September 40-year sale drew the strongest demand since 2020 and the 2026-09-30 two-year cleared at 1.964%. The only live datapoints are small and offsetting: a Canadian monthly budget balance of -C$4.77bn against +C$0.99bn prior, and Japanese yields falling 2.5-4bp across the curve on 2026-09-30 on a fiscal-reassurance report. Neither moves a cross whose daily range is measured in tens of pips. No budget event falls inside the tactical window on either side.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the fiscal differential is the one structural factor favouring the Canadian dollar, and it has a dated Japanese trigger that Canada does not match. Japan's fiscal-monetary circularity is closing precisely as the Takaichi administration wants to spend: the 10-year has risen 141bp in a year to 3.06% and the 30-year sits at 4.15%, and with a 260%-of-GDP stock each 100bp on the average yield eventually costs roughly 2% of GDP in debt service. The FY2027 budget compiles in December with Fitch publicly committed to reviewing the growth-versus-discipline balance, and a 222bp 2s30s spread says the market is increasingly pricing term premium rather than policy. The currency transmission inverts at that point — rising JGB yields are yen-positive when they reflect normalisation and yen-negative when they reflect sovereign risk. Canada's trajectory is also deteriorating, with general government debt on a 91.8% to 98.5% path against an AA median of 49.6% and a 2025-26 deficit of 2.5% of GDP, but from a level that remains a strength and with a federal stock near 42%. Confidence is only 50 because the Japanese ratings are stable, domestic ownership remains the shock absorber it has been for thirty years, and the Canadian evidence base rests on a 322-day-old Fitch assessment.

Confidence is only 50 because thirty years of evidence says Japanese fiscal risk never becomes market-relevant.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/JPY is the highest-volatility CAD cross and among the more volatile JPY crosses, with 60-day realised volatility of 8.52% carried identically in both dossiers. Against that, the gated store's 3-month at-the-money estimate is 7.84% at a 99.7-day tenor, observed 2026-09-30 — which is below realised even before accounting for the known downward bias of the triangle method, which has run 8.7-17.8% light against direct quotes. The honest reading is that volatility is not cheap in absolute terms but is probably underpriced relative to delivery, which argues for spot or forward expression over paying premium. Structurally the cross has no listed option anywhere, so there is no risk reversal, no barrier map and no vol term structure to read — the surface quoted here is an estimate built from the two USD legs and their realised correlation of 0.4587, not a market. Liquidity is a second-tier consideration: CAD/JPY is a liquid enough cross in G10 terms but is materially thinner than either USD leg, and the yen side carries gap risk by design because a second coordinated intervention produces a discontinuity rather than a drift. This factor supplies execution context, not direction, and at a 0.05 weight it contributes nothing to the score.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is abundant and dollar strength is uniform, which for a cross means it mostly cancels. SOFR printed 3.88% on 2026-09-29 on USD 2.967tn of volume with a 16bp first-to-99th percentile spread, reserve balances stand at USD 2.93tn, quantitative tightening ended on 2025-12-01 and reserve-management purchases have grown the balance sheet since — there is no funding stress to transmit to either leg. The broad dollar index rose 1.884 points over the month to 120.33, and both currencies lost ground to the dollar: USD/CAD rose 2.42% while USD/JPY fell 1.54%, so the dollar's strength was actually absorbed asymmetrically, with the yen outperforming it. That is the point — a strong-dollar regime is not a clean signal for this cross because the yen has demonstrated it can rally against a rising dollar on policy and positioning while the Canadian dollar cannot. The pair-specific funding read is the cross-currency basis, and it is a documented gap on both legs: no quoted 3-month CAD/USD or JPY/USD basis was located, and the only derived proxies are the futures roll premia, which conflate basis with the rate differential. With no stress, no divergence in funding availability and no measurable basis, this is a Neutral at modest confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the funding channel stops being symmetric because one leg has a hedge-cost mechanism and the other does not. Japanese institutions hedge 50-60% of roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of foreign assets at 3-4% annual cost, and with the JGB 10-year at 3.06% and the 30-year at 4.15% long-dated domestic paper now out-yields currency-hedged US Treasuries — a crossover that removes a persistent structural yen seller and replaces it with a buyer. The Fed's own September projections put the end-2026 median at 4.1%, implying one more move and then a plateau, which caps hedge costs precisely when every BoJ hike improves the domestic alternative. Canada has no analogous mechanism: Canadian banks source significant USD funding cross-border, the CAD/USD basis is typically tight, so Canada neither benefits from a squeeze nor is protected from its absence, and both sides of the dollar smile are documented as CAD-negative in the base dossier. The offsets are real — December year-end dollar demand widens the basis seasonally, Japan's 550 billion dollar US investment package is a structural dollar bid, and the dollar sits on the exceptionalism side of the smile — which is why confidence is only 52 and why the weekly Japanese securities data have not yet confirmed a linear repatriation trend.

tactical.score_interpretation: At -0.1020 the tactical score clears the Bearish threshold by two thousandths of a point, which is as marginal as this framework gets. The reading is a weak Bearish for CAD/JPY — the pair falls, the yen appreciates — and it is produced by one large negative and two meaningful positives rather than by breadth. Policy & Rates alone contributes -0.1440 at a 0.24 weight, with Guidance at -0.0420 and Event Risk at -0.0290 behind it, against +0.0580 from External Balance and +0.0550 from Flows & Positioning. Five factors contribute exactly zero and together carry 0.44 of the weight: Inflation & Growth, Risk Appetite, Fiscal, Market Structure and USD Liquidity. The honest characterisation is that the tactical verdict rests almost entirely on the rate and guidance channel and is nearly cancelled by terms of trade and crowded positioning; a four-point change in any one of the three largest contributing confidences flips it to Neutral.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights this pair is decided by Policy & Rates at 0.24, Inflation & Growth at 0.18 and the three 0.10 blocks — Risk Appetite, Flows and External Balance — which together carry 0.72 of the book, and of those only Policy & Rates generates a strong directional signal. The weighted score of -0.1020 therefore describes a narrow verdict, not a confident one. The dominant mechanism is a +100bp policy differential that is pointed the wrong way for the currency earning it: the Bank of Canada has held for seven consecutive meetings at the bottom of its neutral band while the Bank of Japan has delivered 50bp in 2026, and the market nonetheless prices the gap to widen, with implied policy rates for late January 2027 of roughly 2.65% for the BoC against roughly 1.56% for the BoJ. The two dossiers reinforce each other here rather than conflict: Canada's own operational core is 1.95% against 112bp of hike premium in its two-year, while Japan's core of 1.7% sits beneath a 7.6% producer pipeline that government subsidy is holding down. Guidance compounds it, because Governor Macklem conditioned his hawkish turn on oil near USD 100 and WTI closed at USD 91.51, while the BoJ's Summary of Opinions shows a majority favouring further hikes against an October move priced at only 25-38%. The bilateral factors that modify the standalone views both push back. Terms of trade is a genuine and durable positive for the pair — Japan runs a fourth consecutive monthly goods deficit with crude imports up 58.7% while Canada posts its first current account surplus since 2022 — though Canada captures only about three quarters of the move it is credited with, realising USD 76.70 a barrel against a USD 100.17 headline. Positioning is the second: specs are short CAD and long JPY simultaneously, so the implied cross position is a crowded short CAD/JPY, which is a squeeze risk running directly against the thesis. What is priced against what we expect is the edge: a widening differential and a BoC that follows through, against our expectation of a hawkish Canadian hold with a lowered oil assumption on 2026-10-28 meeting a Japanese Outlook Report on 2026-10-30 that the curve underpays. The path of least resistance is a drift lower in the pair that only resolves at the end of the window, because both catalysts land in its final days. Conviction is 2 and not 3 because 0.44 of the weight abstains, because the score sits two thousandths from Neutral, and because a short position pays roughly 9 pips a month in roll to wait for a catalyst it cannot reach until 2026-10-30.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: On the two dossiers' own tactical scores, CAD at -0.2576 ranks 9th of 11 and JPY at -0.0281 ranks 5th, a 0.23-point spread that makes short CAD/JPY a credible but not a first-choice expression. Among CAD shorts it ranks behind long USD/CAD (+0.378 against CAD) and long AUD/CAD (+0.304), and roughly level with CAD/NOK and CAD/SGD; the base dossier's own preferred bearish-CAD expression is CAD/NOK, where a 225bp carry disadvantage is compounded by a positive futures roll, against a CAD/JPY short that pays 100bp of carry to wait. Among JPY longs it ranks second-best, behind only long JPY against EUR and CHF on score, but ahead of the AUD and NZD crosses on risk-adjusted terms because this pair's commodity channel partly offsets rather than amplifies the yen view.

strategic.score_interpretation: At -0.2887 the strategic score is a moderate Bearish reading for CAD/JPY and is 2.8 times the tactical magnitude. It is also far better built: seven factors contribute negatively, two positively and only one abstains. Policy & Rates leads at -0.1632, followed by Guidance at -0.0744, Inflation & Growth at -0.0550, USD Liquidity at -0.0416 and Risk Appetite at -0.0364, with Flows and Event Risk adding -0.0300 and -0.0275. The two positives are substantial and are what hold conviction at 3: External Balance contributes +0.1044 at the second-largest weight in the book, and Fiscal & Sovereign adds +0.0350 on Japan's December budget risk. Strip the terms-of-trade offset out and the score would be near -0.39; that single factor is the whole of the uncertainty in this call.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the book is decided by Policy & Rates at 0.24, External Balance at 0.18 and the two 0.12 blocks, Guidance and Inflation & Growth — 0.64 of the weight in four factors, three of which are negative for the pair and the fourth of which is the single largest positive. The net score of -0.2887 therefore has real breadth behind it rather than resting on one channel. The dominant mechanism is the composition of the rate differential rather than its level: the Bank of Canada sits at 2.25%, the bottom of its own 2.25-3.25% neutral band, with an operational core of 1.95%, unemployment at 6.4%, wage growth halved to 2.0% and a tariff regime that escalated to import bans on 2026-09-29, while the Bank of Japan has delivered 50bp in 2026 and holds three decisions inside the window including Outlook Reports on 2026-10-30 and 2027-01-22. Two Japanese hikes against a Canadian hold halves the bilateral differential from 100bp to 50bp, and the Canadian two-year carries 112bp of premium above its policy rate that a shortfall would force out. The two dossiers reinforce rather than conflict — CAD scores last of eleven strategically at -0.3646 while JPY scores third at +0.2497 — and the bilateral factors mostly deepen that rather than moderating it: Japanese institutional repatriation driven by the hedged-yield crossover has no Canadian counterpart, the coordinated US-Japan intervention put truncates the yen's weak tail without truncating its strong one, and Canada's USMCA now runs on annual review cycles through 2036. The genuine conflict is terms of trade, and it is large: at a 0.18 weight a Japanese goods deficit running for four consecutive months with crude imports up 58.7%, against a Canadian current account surplus on record energy exports, is worth +0.1044 and is the reason this is a conviction-3 call rather than a conviction-4 one. What is priced is a differential widening into late January and a current account surplus that persists; what we expect is a differential of 50-75bp by end-Q1 2027 and a Canadian surplus shrinking toward C$2-5bn as WTI converges on the USD 83.90 consensus — which, note, erodes the pair's one supporting factor at the same time as it removes Canada's inflation case. The path of least resistance is a stepped decline keyed to the Japanese forecast rounds, with the December FY2027 budget the main two-sided interruption. Dated catalysts are the BoC on 2026-10-28 and 2026-12-09, the BoJ on 2026-10-30, 2026-12-18 and 2027-01-22, and USTR's end-2026 USMCA target. Conviction is 3 because three independent channels — policy compression, guidance divergence and Japanese institutional flow — point the same way against one large and genuinely uncertain commodity offset, and because the published bank forecasts sit flat to higher on this cross, so being right means being right against the sell side.

Short CAD/JPY therefore ranks second among all CAD-short expressions, behind CAD/NOK and marginally ahead of CAD/SEK, and it ranks first among all JPY-long expressions because the Canadian dollar is the weakest counterpart in the strategic set. The handicap relative to CAD/NOK is carry and roll: short CAD/NOK is paid 225bp plus a positive futures roll to wait, while short CAD/JPY pays 100bp of policy carry and roughly 111bp of annualised roll, so the pair needs to be right faster.

Both bank documents predate the 2026-09-18 BoJ hike in part and are flagged as stale on that basis. Extrapolation sites were excluded as a category error, not as a weak source.
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Weak Bearish on the pair, net -0.1020, conviction 2 — a lower CAD/JPY over two to four weeks, but with the move concentrated at the very end of the window because both resolving events fall on 2026-10-28 and 2026-10-30, and with a crowded short CAD/JPY positioning base arguing the pair can squeeze higher first.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish on the pair, net -0.2887, conviction 3 — a materially lower CAD/JPY over one to six months, driven by a bilateral policy differential compressing from 100bp toward 50-75bp, Japanese institutional repatriation with no Canadian counterpart, and a Canadian trade-policy risk premium that is now architectural.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Below consensus on both horizons. RBC has the cross rising from 110 to 114 through 2027 and the aggregator has it at 113.71 by Q1 2027; TD alone is close to flat at 111.3. We are directionally opposed to the first two and modestly below the third.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Roughly 3 to 4 yen below the aggregated Q1 2027 figure of 113.71 and 1 to 2 yen below RBC's Q1 2027 mark of 112, on a 110.77 spot. Against the forward curve the divergence is larger still in the same direction: the futures-implied roll of -111.2bp annualised already prices the cross below spot, and our view is for spot to undershoot that. Pass 2 quantifies it: 108.20 against 113.71 is 551 pips; against RBC's 112 it is 380 pips; against the 6M forward of 110.155 it is 196 pips.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three specific weightings. First, the rate channel: consensus and the curve both price the bilateral differential to widen into late January, on implied policy rates near 2.65% for the Bank of Canada and 1.56% for the Bank of Japan, while we read the Canadian two-year's 112bp of hike premium as unsupported by a 1.95% operational core and the BoJ's 25-38% October pricing as underpaying a Bank whose Summary of Opinions shows a hawkish median. Second, the current account: consensus capitalises Canada's C$8.8bn Q2 surplus as structural and reads Japan's 5.03%-of-GDP headline as yen support, where we treat the first as a reversing oil-price effect capped by a USD 14.80 WCS discount and the second as primary income reinvested offshore with the FX-generative goods line in deficit. Third, flows: the hedged-yield crossover that now makes long JGBs beat currency-hedged Treasuries after 3-4% hedge costs is absent from essentially every published cross forecast, and it is a persistent yen buyer with no Canadian analogue.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The pair falls through the bank path rather than toward it, so the error compounds: being right by 3 to 4 yen against the Q1 2027 aggregate is a 3% relative move on a cross with 8.5% realised volatility. The cleaner relative-value payoff, given that a short CAD/JPY pays 100bp of carry and roughly 111bp of annualised roll to wait, is to pair it against a short CAD/NOK, where the same Canadian view is expressed with a positive carry.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: Two distinct ways to lose. The first is the commodity path: a Hormuz re-escalation that pushes WTI back above USD 100 while the Brent-WTI spread narrows restores Canada's revenue capture, the Bank of Canada's own stated hiking precondition and Japan's import bill shock simultaneously, which is the single scenario that flips the largest positive factor and the largest negative one at once. The second is a BoJ that stalls at 1.25% through 2027-01-22 under political pressure while the Bank of Canada delivers against its curve, which leaves a short position paying 100bp of carry plus roll for nothing.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons agree in direction and disagree sharply in strength, and the composition is where the information sits. Tactically the case rests on a single channel — Policy & Rates and Guidance together supply -0.1860 of a -0.1020 net — and is nearly cancelled by a crowded short CAD/JPY positioning base and a live terms-of-trade tailwind, with 0.44 of the weight abstaining. Strategically seven of ten factors turn negative as Inflation & Growth, Risk Appetite, Flows and USD Liquidity each flip against the pair for mechanical reasons: the Canadian gasoline base effect rolls off while the Japanese energy subsidy expires, credit starts from the floor of its range, the speculative positioning extreme normalises leaving Japanese institutional repatriation as the residual flow, and the hedged-yield crossover keeps working. The two things capping the tactical case are both short-lived, while the two driving it are structural.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 2026-10-28 Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report followed by the 2026-10-30 Bank of Japan decision with Outlook Report. Those two days are where the tactical and strategic theses become the same trade: Canada must publish an oil assumption against a USD 100 threshold its own commodity has already failed, and Japan gets its first scheduled chance to mark up a CPI path the curve prices at 25-38%. The crowded short CAD/JPY positioning base is also most likely to have normalised by then, historically four to eight weeks after an extreme.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The direction does not need to be re-established across the transition, but the sizing does. Tactically the score sits two thousandths from Neutral with a positioning squeeze risk and a roll cost of roughly 9 pips a month, so the position deserves to be small and patient until 2026-10-30. Strategically the case broadens materially and the same position can carry more weight, with the December FY2027 Japanese budget and any USTR interim USMCA agreement the two events most likely to interrupt it. Pass-2 levels for that sequencing: build the tactical half-unit on rallies into 111.40–112.00 before 2026-10-28. Add the strategic unit only after the October cluster, either on a retest of 110.72–111.41 from below or on a daily close below 108.92. The 200-week average reaches the eight-touch band by mid-December, so a break of that band after year-end has to beat two levels at once.

forward_vs_spot.forward_1m: 110.668 outright (-10.3 pips, -1.112% annualised); our expected 1M rate 109.40, edge +127 pips for a short
forward_vs_spot.edge_3m: +146 pips for a short (forward 110.463 vs expected 109.00). Forwards are derived linearly from the CME 6C/6J roll of -111.2bp annualised (observed 2026-09-30, 19.6–47.7-day tenor), not quoted points, and bundle the 100bp policy differential with about 11bp of basis and term effect.
forward_vs_spot.edge_6m: +196 pips for a short (forward 110.155 vs expected 108.20). The edge is largest in absolute terms at six months but front-loaded per month because the October double event does most of the work and the 200-week floor slows the rest. If spot simply holds at 110.77, a short loses the roll of 10/31/62 pips at one, three and six months.

catalysts.event: Canada merchandise trade balance (August) and Ivey PMI (September)
catalysts.rationale: The July balance collapsed to +C$0.77bn from +C$4.2bn with exports to the US down 6.6%, and this is the first print covering a full month of the 50% Section 338 duty regime. Because the bullish case for CAD/JPY rests almost entirely on Canada's terms of trade against a Japanese goods deficit, a further narrowing attacks the pair's single supporting factor directly rather than at one remove.

catalysts.event: Japan current account and adjusted current account (August)
catalysts.rationale: The July surplus of 2,988.9bn yen rested on primary income of 4,289.6bn that is reinvested offshore, while the goods line ran a fourth consecutive deficit. For this pair the composition matters more than the headline: a widening goods deficit on crude imports up 58.7% is CAD/JPY-positive through the settlement channel even as a larger headline surplus reads as yen-supportive to the market.

catalysts.event: Canada Labour Force Survey (September), released alongside US non-farm payrolls
catalysts.rationale: August employment fell 41,700 with wage growth halved to 2.0%. A second negative print pushes the unemployment rate above 6.6% and forces hike premium out of a Canadian two-year carrying 112bp above the policy rate, which compresses the bilateral differential directly. The simultaneous US release means the pair trades the Canadian number through a dollar filter on the base leg only.

Headline at 3.0% is sustained by gasoline at +22.8% against a trim-median average of 1.95%. A decay toward 2.7-2.9% with core unchanged is a downside surprise against roughly 120bp of tightening in the curve, and it narrows the operational-core differential against a Japanese core of 1.7% to almost nothing — removing the inflation justification for the pair's 100bp carry.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report, debuting a new inflation model
catalysts.rationale: The highest-leverage Canadian date in the horizon and the first half of a two-day double event. The Bank must publish an oil assumption against the Governor's stated USD 100 threshold while WTI trades at USD 91.51, and it reports two days before the BoJ, so a dovish Canadian revision sets the tone into a Japanese meeting the market prices as a hold. Sequence amplifies rather than offsets.

The Fed meets the same day as the Bank of Canada. For a non-USD cross the effect is indirect and runs through both legs: a retained hiking bias supports the dollar against both currencies, but the September evidence is that the yen can outperform a rising dollar while the Canadian dollar cannot, so a hawkish hold leans mildly against the pair rather than being neutral for it.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: The single most important date for the quote leg and the second half of the double event. A quarterly forecast round at which the Bank can raise its CPI path, against a market pricing only 25-38% for a 25bp move and a Summary of Opinions in which a majority favour further hikes. A delivered hike takes the bilateral differential from 100bp to 75bp in one session; even a hawkish hold reprices December, which is currently near 39%. (Pass 2: the pair rose 70 pips on the day of the fully expected 2026-09-18 hike, so the Outlook Report's forecast path matters more than the decision itself.)

catalysts.event: Japan national CPI (October) — released week 3 of November (added in pass 2; exact day not stated, third Friday assumed)
catalysts.rationale: Core CPI excluding fresh food has run below target for seven months at 1.7%, beneath a 7.6% producer pipeline that electricity subsidies are holding down. A print that starts to show pass-through raises December hike pricing and compresses the bilateral differential in expectation. That matters more for CAD/JPY than for USD/JPY, because the Canadian leg is moving the other way on the gasoline base effect.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision (no Monetary Policy Report) and FOMC decision with SEP
catalysts.rationale: If the Bank of Canada has still not moved by this meeting the market's roughly two-hikes-by-January pricing becomes untenable and the 112bp of premium in the Canadian two-year is most likely to be given back. For the pair that is a direct compression of the base leg's yield advantage with no offsetting Japanese event in the same week.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 budget compilation and Fitch review window — week 3 of December (added in pass 2; exact day not stated)
catalysts.rationale: This is the one Japanese event that could push the pair up. A budget that reprices the JGB long end as term premium rather than normalisation turns higher yields into a yen negative. National Bank notes the long end already carries extra term premium tied to fiscal concerns. Fiscal & Sovereign is the strategic factor scored Bullish for the pair on exactly this risk.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting (no Outlook Report)
catalysts.rationale: The second Japanese hike opportunity in the window, priced at roughly 39%. If October delivers a hold with a hawkish forecast revision this becomes the market's focal point and pricing should converge higher through November, which compresses the differential in expectation before any move is delivered. A bare statement moves the pair less than an Outlook Report, so the content is in the guidance.

catalysts.event: USTR target date for USMCA interim agreements
catalysts.rationale: The United States declined the 16-year USMCA extension on 2026-07-01, placing the agreement on annual reviews through 2036, and USTR has stated it aims for interim deals by end-2026. An agreement that suspends the Section 338 import bans is the largest single upside catalyst for the base leg and the principal risk to this verdict, because it would remove the standing Canadian risk premium that the Event Risk factor scores against the pair.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: The second Japanese projection round inside the window and the end point of the strategic horizon. By this meeting two of three hike opportunities will have passed, so it is where a stalled normalisation would become visible and where a terminal rate above 1.75% would first be signalled. It is also the date against which the market currently prices a BoJ rate of roughly 1.56%, which our view says is too low.

catalysts.event: Japanese fiscal year-end repatriation window (added in pass 2)
catalysts.rationale: The best-documented seasonal yen-positive flow falls inside the strategic window and this year overlaps a live structural repatriation trend. Bank of America sees scope for Japanese institutions to bring more capital home as domestic bond yields become increasingly attractive. For CAD/JPY it is the most likely flow to push the pair through the eight-touch band and the rising 200-week average late in the horizon.

invalidators.mechanism: The pair's only fundamental support, the carry, would then be widening and the guidance-divergence factor would reverse.

invalidators.mechanism: Canada's revenue capture and the BoC's own hiking precondition come back together while Japan's import bill rises, flipping the largest negative factor and strengthening the largest positive one on this specific cross.

invalidators.condition: The BoJ holds at 1.25% on both 2026-10-30 and 2026-12-18 with no upward revision to its Outlook Report CPI path
invalidators.mechanism: The compression mechanism disappears and a short is left paying about 62 pips of roll over six months for nothing.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: BoJ statements, Outlook Report core CPI forecasts, OIS pricing for 2027-01-22 below 30%

invalidators.mechanism: The pair would have recovered its full medium-term structure against the fundamental view, which would be evidence that the positioning and terms-of-trade offsets are dominating the rate channel.

invalidators.mechanism: It removes the standing Canadian risk premium scored in Event Risk and the trade drag weighing on Canada's external balance, while Japan has no offsetting event.

assumptions: Price series as delivered. The payload states dataPoints 130, dateRange '2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02', spot 110.77119 and spotDate '2026-10-02'. The dataQuality array reads verbatim: 'CAD/JPY: 4899 weekday bars in the store (2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02); 1007 weekly, 500 monthly; 130 daily bars passed downstream (2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02), which is the 1-6 month strategic horizon'. The computation range for averages and zones is 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02 (4,899 weekday bars), with zero weekend bars dropped.

Spot date versus valuation date. The spotDate (2026-10-02) is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date. Every level, pip distance, percentage, target and forward in this report is anchored to 110.77119, and no web-quoted spot was substituted. The pass-1 verdict was scored on the same reference.

Direction inputs. Factor stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, contributions, net scores, convictions, rationales, rankings, consensus divergence and cross-horizon consistency are carried verbatim from the pass-1 Direction Verdict. Pass-2 additions are clearly labelled. The one dissent is in Factor 9: a chart-informed tactical stance would probably lean Bearish, worth at most about -0.025, which was not applied. The pass-1 one-month figure of -3.86% is the dossiers' 2026-09-29 window; the payload's one-month figure is -1.94%.

Moving averages. All are simple averages of weekday closes. The 200-week SMA slope (+0.039471/week) and weeksSinceCloseAbove200w (0) come from the payload. How long spot has been above the 200-week average is not supplied; the roughly one-year estimate is a back-extrapolation and is flagged as an inference. Convergence timings assume a constant slope.

Zones. All zones come from the payload's clustered weekly and monthly swing closes. Distances are measured to the nearest zone boundary. No web-sourced support or resistance levels are used. The only chart pattern cited (a medium-term rising-channel break) is from Investtech's automated analysis dated 2026-09-04.

Implied volatility. The 8.17% / 7.84% / 7.813% term structure is the store's triangle estimate (realised correlation 0.4587). It is not a quote and is known to run 8.7–17.8% low. The bias-corrected 3M range of about 8.6–9.5% is a pass-2 calculation. There are no listed options, risk reversals or barrier data on the cross, and no implied-vol history, so no IV percentile. Skew direction is inferred from the two USD legs, using stale or indirect observations.

Forwards. Outrights are derived linearly from the -111.2bp CME 6C/6J roll (observed 2026-09-30) and are not quoted points. The roll embeds the cross-currency basis, which is a documented gap on both legs.

Rates. Policy rates are from the payload: CAD 2.25% as of 2026-09-28; JPY 1.25% as of 2026-09-29. The 10-year yields in the payload are monthly vintages dated 2026-08-01 (CAD 3.675%, JPY 2.94%) and are never quoted as live. Live spreads use the dossiers' 2026-09-28/30 prints. The 2-year spread signpost uses Canada 3.37% and JGB 1.93% from the dossiers.

Scenarios and risk/reward. Probabilities follow the framework's 50/25/25 template. Targets sit on payload zones. Expected values are gross of roll, with the net figure shown separately. Sizing guidance is in relative risk units, scaled to ATR(14) of 80 pips, with a gap allowance for the yen leg's intervention risk.

Consensus. The RBC and TD figures are carried from pass 1 and are partly stale. Exchange Rates UK is an aggregator, refreshed in this pass. Extrapolation and model sites found in research (Traders Union, gov.capital, CoinCodex, WalletInvestor and similar) were excluded as a category error.
Bilateral trade. IMF DOTS 2024 figures are used as supplied. The two countries' reported figures disagree, and both are shown.

Formatter notes: the source report does not state a CFTC percentile for either leg or an implied-volatility percentile (it states none can be computed), so base_cftc_percentile, quote_cftc_percentile and iv_percentile are null rather than invented. The source report does not state dossier dates, so both are set to the 2026-10-01 valuation date. Two catalysts the report dates only to a week ('2026-11-W3', '2026-12-W3') carry approximate calendar dates (2026-11-20, 2026-12-15) to satisfy the date format.
